title: The Case Toolkit
summary: 30 frameworks that crack almost every business case, each with a plain summary, a diagram of how it works and a storyboard showing how to put it on one clean slide.

chapters.title: How to use this guide
chapters.markdown:
A **framework** is a ready-made checklist that splits a messy business question into a few smaller questions we can answer one at a time. This guide covers the 30 frameworks that, between them, fit almost every case we will meet in an interview, a case competition or a first job.

Most students learn frameworks as lists to recite. Judges and interviewers do not reward the list; they reward the answer the list helped us find, shown on a clean slide. Hence every framework here comes with two pictures: how the framework is built, and how to storyboard it on a single slide with plenty of white space.

### How each framework is laid out

1. **In one line:** a plain definition, so we can explain it to anyone in ten seconds.
2. **Use it when:** the kind of case question that should make us reach for it.
3. **The parts:** each building block with a short explanation and an everyday e.g.
4. **The framework:** a diagram of how the parts fit together.
5. **On a slide:** a storyboard of the slide: where the title, the visual, the highlight and the takeaway sit, and how much space to leave empty.
6. **Watch out:** the one mistake people make most often with it.

### The six groups

![The 30 frameworks at a glance](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/i00_map.png)

1. **Structure the problem:** the two habits that sit under every other framework.
2. **Follow the money:** profit, revenue, cost, pricing and the numbers behind them.
3. **Grow and enter:** sizing a market, entering it, launching into it, buying into it.
4. **Read the competition:** the industry, the rivals, and where the company stands.
5. **Win the customer:** who to serve, what to offer and how they move from stranger to fan.
6. **Look inside the company:** how the business is built and run.

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "A note on the numbers", "icon": "fa-calculator", "text": "All companies, figures and slide titles in the examples are made up for teaching. Real brand names appear only as everyday examples."}
```

> **Download the whole guide:** [The Case Toolkit (PDF)](content/prep/files/case-toolkit.pdf)

chapters.title: Slides with white space
chapters.markdown:
A **storyboard** is a rough sketch of a slide drawn before we open PowerPoint: one box per idea, the title written as a full sentence, and everything else left empty on purpose.

![Anatomy of a clean case slide](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/i00_anatomy.png)

### Seven rules for every slide

1. **One slide, one message:** The title is the answer, written as a sentence of 15 words or fewer. If we cannot write the title, the slide is not ready. e.g. "Rising fuel cost, not falling fares, explains 80% of the profit drop" beats "Profitability analysis".
2. **Leave a frame of empty space:** Keep a clear margin of about 5% of the slide width on every side, and never let a box touch the edge. Thus the eye rests and the content looks deliberate, not crammed.
3. **The framework is the picture:** Draw the framework itself as the visual (the tree, the 2x2, the funnel) instead of a wall of bullets. Hence the judge sees the structure of our thinking in one glance.
4. **Grey everything, colour one thing:** Draw all boxes in grey and put colour only on the part that holds the answer. e.g. in a five forces slide, only the strongest force is coral. So the eye goes straight to the point.
5. **A takeaway the judge can read alone:** Give the "so what" its own box with two or three short lines at most. If someone only reads the title and this box, they should still get the story.
6. **Line things up:** Use at most two or three columns, align every box to the same left edge and top line, and keep gaps between boxes equal. Thus the slide feels calm even when it holds a lot.
7. **Source at the bottom, small:** Put the source or the key assumption in a thin footer line. This keeps the numbers honest without stealing space from the message.

![Five steps from framework to slide](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/i00_flow.png)

chapters.title: Issue tree and MECE
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

An **issue tree** breaks one big question into smaller questions that are **MECE**: mutually exclusive (no overlap) and collectively exhaustive (nothing left out).

### Use it when

Always. It is the first thing we draw in any case, and every other framework in this guide is really a ready-made issue tree.

### The parts

1. **The key question:** One clear question at the root, with a number and a deadline where possible. e.g. "How can a café chain raise profit by 20% in two years?"
2. **Branches:** Split the question into two to four parts that do not overlap. e.g. profit splits cleanly into revenue and cost, so nothing is counted twice.
3. **Sub-branches:** Keep splitting until each box can be answered with one piece of data or one interview. This is where the analysis actually happens.
4. **The MECE check:** Ask two questions of every split: do any boxes overlap, and is anything missing? e.g. splitting customers into "students" and "young people" overlaps, hence it fails.
5. **Prioritise:** Mark the two or three branches most likely to hold the answer and start there. Thus we do not spend time on branches that cannot move the result.

### The framework

![Issue tree and MECE: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f01_issue-tree.png)

### On a slide

![Issue tree and MECE: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s01_issue-tree.png)

1. Title states the answer the tree led to, not the word "Issue tree"
2. Tree runs left to right with equal gaps; three branches only
3. The branch with the answer is coral, the rest stay grey
4. So-what box sits on the right with two short lines

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Building a tree that is neat but not tied to the question. Every branch must be able to change the answer, otherwise cut it."}
```

chapters.title: Pyramid principle and hypothesis
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **pyramid principle** means we lead with the answer, then give the three or so reasons that support it, then the facts under each reason; a **hypothesis** is our best early guess at that answer.

### Use it when

When we present any recommendation, and at the start of a case to decide which branch of the tree to test first.

### The parts

1. **Answer first:** Open with the recommendation in one sentence. e.g. "Launch the snack in tier-2 cities first."
2. **Key reasons:** Give three reasons, each a full sentence, and keep them MECE. e.g. demand is growing faster there, rivals are weaker, and our distributors already reach those stores.
3. **Supporting facts:** Under each reason sit the data, interviews or examples that prove it. This lets the listener stop at any level and still get the point.
4. **Hypothesis:** Before the data, state what we think the answer is and what would prove us wrong. Thus we collect only the data that can confirm or kill the guess.
5. **Test and update:** If the facts disagree, change the hypothesis, not the facts. Hence the pyramid at the end can look very different from the guess at the start.

### The framework

![Pyramid principle and hypothesis: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f02_pyramid.png)

### On a slide

![Pyramid principle and hypothesis: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s02_pyramid.png)

1. The title is the answer and names all three reasons
2. Three equal columns, one reason each, same height
3. Answer box is the only coloured box
4. Facts sit as one or two short lines under each column, not paragraphs

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Telling the story in the order we did the work (\"first we looked at...\"). Judges want the answer first, the journey never."}
```

chapters.title: Profitability framework
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **profitability framework** explains a change in profit by splitting it into revenue (price × volume) and cost (fixed + variable), then finding which piece moved.

### Use it when

Whenever a case says profit, margin or earnings have fallen, or a client wants them to rise.

### The parts

1. **Revenue = price × volume:** Check whether we are selling at a lower price or selling fewer units. e.g. a cinema chain may hold ticket prices but sell fewer tickets as people stream at home.
2. **Revenue mix:** Split revenue by product, customer or region to see which part moved. e.g. popcorn may earn more margin than tickets, so a shift in mix changes profit even when sales look flat.
3. **Fixed cost:** Costs that stay the same whatever we sell, such as rent and salaries. When volume falls, these are spread over fewer units, hence the margin shrinks.
4. **Variable cost:** Costs that rise with every unit, such as raw material and delivery. e.g. a rise in milk prices hits every cup a café sells.
5. **Compare and isolate:** Compare each piece against last year and against rivals, and find the one that moved most. Thus we explain the drop before we try to fix it.

### The framework

![Profitability framework: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f03_profitability.png)

### On a slide

![Profitability framework: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s03_profitability.png)

1. Title names the driver and its share of the problem
2. Profit tree on the left, only two levels deep
3. Only the cost branch that moved is coloured
4. Takeaway box pairs the cause with the fix

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Jumping to \"cut costs\" before checking revenue. Many profit problems are price or mix problems in disguise."}
```

chapters.title: Revenue growth framework
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **revenue growth framework** lists every way a company can earn more: more customers, more per customer, more often, or new products and markets.

### Use it when

When the case asks how to grow sales, double revenue, or hit a growth target.

### The parts

1. **More customers:** Win new buyers through new channels, regions or segments. e.g. a D2C skincare brand entering modern retail stores.
2. **Higher spend per visit:** Raise the bill through price, bundles or upselling. e.g. a fast-food chain offering a meal upgrade for ₹49.
3. **More frequent visits:** Bring the same customers back more often through loyalty or subscriptions. e.g. a coffee chain's app that rewards every fifth cup.
4. **Keep customers longer:** Reduce churn so fewer customers leave. This is often cheaper than finding new ones, hence it is worth checking early.
5. **New products or markets:** Sell something new, or sell abroad. This is the slowest and riskiest lever, thus it usually comes last.

### The framework

![Revenue growth framework: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f04_revenue-growth.png)

### On a slide

![Revenue growth framework: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s04_revenue-growth.png)

1. Title names the lever and its size in rupees
2. Three branches, each with two leaves only
3. Winning lever in coral; leave the rest grey
4. Payback number in the so-what box, nothing else

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Listing all levers equally. Size each one with a rough number, because the biggest lever is the recommendation."}
```

chapters.title: Cost reduction framework
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **cost reduction framework** maps every cost from input to customer, sizes each one, and cuts where the cost is large, rising, or higher than rivals.

### Use it when

When the client needs to save a set amount, margins trail rivals, or a price war is coming.

### The parts

1. **Map the cost base:** List costs along the value chain: buying, making, moving, selling, support. e.g. for a bakery: flour, ovens, delivery vans, shop rent, head office.
2. **Size each bucket:** Show each cost as a share of revenue. The biggest buckets matter most, hence a 10% cut in a big bucket beats a 50% cut in a tiny one.
3. **Benchmark:** Compare each bucket with rivals or with last year. e.g. if our delivery cost is 12% of sales and the rival's is 7%, we know where to look.
4. **Find the cause:** Ask whether the cost is high because of price paid, quantity used, or waste. Each cause has a different fix.
5. **Choose fixes:** Renegotiate, redesign, automate, outsource or stop. Thus we pick the fix that saves most with the least harm to customers.

### The framework

![Cost reduction framework: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f05_cost-reduction.png)

### On a slide

![Cost reduction framework: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s05_cost-reduction.png)

1. Title gives the gap and the saving
2. Cost chain runs left to right as one row
3. Only the bucket with the gap is coloured
4. Takeaway strip runs along the bottom, one line

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Cutting what is easy instead of what is big. Always size first, then cut."}
```

chapters.title: Pricing framework
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **pricing framework** sets a price by looking at three numbers: what it costs us (the floor), what rivals charge (the reference) and what the customer would pay (the ceiling).

### Use it when

When the case asks what to charge for a new product, whether to raise or cut prices, or how to respond to a rival's price move.

### The parts

1. **Cost-based (the floor):** Our cost per unit plus a target margin. We should rarely price below this, hence it is the floor.
2. **Competitor-based (the reference):** What similar products sell for. e.g. a new bottled water must sit close to the ₹20 that buyers already expect.
3. **Value-based (the ceiling):** What the product is worth to the customer, often the money or time it saves them. e.g. software that saves a factory ₹10 lakh a year can charge far more than it costs to make.
4. **Pick the point:** Set the price between floor and ceiling, closer to the ceiling when we are clearly better. Thus we keep value for ourselves instead of giving it away.
5. **Check the reaction:** Ask how customers and rivals will respond. e.g. a price cut a rival can match quickly only lowers everyone's margin.

### The framework

![Pricing framework: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f06_pricing.png)

### On a slide

![Pricing framework: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s06_pricing.png)

1. Title gives the price and why it is safe
2. Price ladder as five bars, lowest to highest
3. Our chosen price is the only coloured bar
4. So-what box gives margin and room to discount

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Pricing from cost alone. Cost tells us the floor, not the price."}
```

chapters.title: Breakeven analysis
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Breakeven** is the number of units we must sell for total revenue to equal total cost, found by dividing fixed cost by the contribution each unit makes.

### Use it when

When the case asks whether a new product, store or investment is worth it, or how long until it pays back.

### The parts

1. **Fixed cost:** Costs that do not change with volume, such as rent, salaries and machines. e.g. a new café pays ₹3 lakh a month whether it sells 10 cups or 1,000.
2. **Contribution per unit:** Price minus variable cost. e.g. a ₹150 coffee with ₹50 of milk, beans and cup contributes ₹100.
3. **Breakeven volume:** Fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit. e.g. ₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹100 = 3,000 cups a month, or 100 a day.
4. **Sanity check:** Compare the breakeven volume with what is realistic. If 100 cups a day is half the footfall of the street, the plan is risky.
5. **Payback period:** For an investment, divide the upfront cost by the monthly profit after breakeven. Thus we know how long our money is at risk.

### The framework

![Breakeven analysis: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f07_breakeven.png)

### On a slide

![Breakeven analysis: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s07_breakeven.png)

1. Title gives the breakeven number and when we hit it
2. One chart: two lines and the crossing point, no gridlines
3. Mark only the breakeven point in colour
4. So-what box checks it against reality

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Forgetting the sanity check. A breakeven number is only useful next to what the market can actually give."}
```

chapters.title: Unit economics (CAC and LTV)
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Unit economics** checks whether one customer is profitable by comparing what they are worth over their life (**LTV**) with what it cost to win them (**CAC**).

### Use it when

For start-ups, apps, subscriptions and any business that spends heavily to acquire customers.

### The parts

1. **Customer acquisition cost (CAC):** Total marketing and sales spend ÷ new customers won. e.g. ₹10 lakh spent to win 2,000 users gives a CAC of ₹500.
2. **Contribution per order:** What we keep from each order after variable costs such as delivery, discounts and payment fees. e.g. a ₹400 grocery order may leave only ₹40.
3. **Lifetime value (LTV):** Contribution per order × orders per year × years they stay. e.g. ₹40 × 24 × 2 = ₹1,920.
4. **LTV to CAC ratio:** A ratio of about 3 or more is healthy; below 1 means every new customer loses money. Hence growth alone can make a business worse.
5. **Payback:** Months of contribution needed to earn back the CAC. Shorter payback means less cash tied up, thus faster safe growth.

### The framework

![Unit economics (CAC and LTV): the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f08_unit-economics.png)

### On a slide

![Unit economics (CAC and LTV): slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s08_unit-economics.png)

1. Title names the leak in the unit economics
2. Waterfall from order value down to contribution
3. The leak is the only coloured bar
4. Ratio and the fix in the so-what box

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Counting revenue, not contribution, in LTV. A customer's value is what we keep, not what they pay."}
```

chapters.title: Market sizing
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Market sizing** estimates how big a market is by multiplying a few reasonable numbers, either from the population down (**top-down**) or from a single store or user up (**bottom-up**).

### Use it when

When the case asks how big a market is, how much a product could sell, or whether a market is worth entering.

### The parts

1. **Define the market:** Say exactly what we are sizing: which product, which customers, where, per year or per month, in units or rupees. This avoids a right answer to the wrong question.
2. **Top-down:** Start from the population and narrow down. e.g. urban households × share with a car × washes per month × price per wash.
3. **Bottom-up:** Start from one unit and scale up. e.g. one car wash serves 40 cars a day × 300 days × ₹300 × number of washes in the city.
4. **Round and state assumptions:** Use round numbers and say each assumption aloud. Thus the interviewer can follow, and correct us early.
5. **Cross-check:** Do both methods, or compare with a known figure. If the two answers are far apart, one assumption is wrong.

### The framework

![Market sizing: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f09_market-sizing.png)

### On a slide

![Market sizing: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s09_market-sizing.png)

1. Title is the number, rounded
2. Funnel narrows step by step, one number per step
3. Colour the least certain assumption
4. Cross-check and the key unknown in the side box

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Precise-looking answers built on hidden assumptions. A round number with clear logic beats a precise number nobody can check."}
```

chapters.title: Market entry
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **market entry framework** decides whether and how a company should enter a new market by checking the market, the competition, our own ability, the entry mode and the money.

### Use it when

When a client asks: should we enter this country, this city, this segment or this product category?

### The parts

1. **Market attractiveness:** Size, growth and profit of the market. e.g. a fast-growing but tiny market may not be worth the effort.
2. **Competition:** Who is there, how strong they are, and what gap they leave. e.g. many small players and no clear leader means room to win.
3. **Our ability to win:** Do we have the brand, product, cost or partners to beat local players? This decides if the market is attractive for us, not just in general.
4. **Entry mode:** Build from scratch, partner, franchise, or buy a local firm. Each trades speed against control and cost.
5. **Financials and risk:** Investment, breakeven and what could go wrong. Thus the answer is a clear yes or no, with conditions.

### The framework

![Market entry: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f10_market-entry.png)

### On a slide

![Market entry: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s10_market-entry.png)

1. Title gives the yes and the how
2. Five checks as one row, in the order we test them
3. Colour the check that changes the decision
4. Bottom strip gives the financial proof

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Stopping at \"the market is attractive\". An attractive market where we have no edge is a trap."}
```

chapters.title: Ansoff matrix
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **Ansoff matrix** sorts growth options into four boxes by asking two things: is the product new or existing, and is the market new or existing?

### Use it when

When the case asks where growth should come from and how risky each path is.

### The parts

1. **Market penetration:** Sell more of the same product to the same market, the safest path. e.g. a tea brand running offers to win share in its home state.
2. **Market development:** Take the same product to a new market. e.g. an Indian snack brand selling to the Indian diaspora in the UK.
3. **Product development:** Sell a new product to existing customers. e.g. a dairy brand adding protein shakes for the same buyers.
4. **Diversification:** A new product for a new market, the riskiest path. Hence it needs the strongest reason.
5. **Read the risk:** Risk grows as we move away from the bottom-left box. Thus we pick the safest box that still meets the growth target.

### The framework

![Ansoff matrix: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f11_ansoff.png)

### On a slide

![Ansoff matrix: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s11_ansoff.png)

1. Title names the box we chose
2. 2x2 with plain axis labels, no arrows inside
3. Chosen box coral; other three grey
4. So-what gives the reason and the size

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Filling all four boxes with ideas and choosing none. The matrix is for comparing risk, so end with a choice."}
```

chapters.title: New product launch (go-to-market)
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

A **go-to-market plan** sets out who we sell a new product to, what we promise them, how we reach them and how we will know it is working.

### Use it when

When the case asks how to launch a product, a brand or a service.

### The parts

1. **Target customer:** The first group who need it most, not everyone. e.g. a new electric scooter targeting college students in one city.
2. **Value proposition:** One sentence on why they should switch. e.g. "Half the running cost of a petrol scooter."
3. **Channels:** Where they will discover and buy it: stores, online, sales team, partners. This should follow where the customer already is.
4. **Price and offer:** Launch price, trial offers and financing. e.g. a ₹999 monthly plan makes a ₹90,000 scooter feel affordable.
5. **Launch plan and metrics:** Phases, budget and the few numbers we track: trials, conversion, repeat. Thus we can scale what works and stop what does not.

### The framework

![New product launch (go-to-market): the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f12_go-to-market.png)

### On a slide

![New product launch (go-to-market): slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s12_go-to-market.png)

1. Title names the first customer and the reason
2. Five steps as one clean row
3. Colour the choice the plan depends on
4. Bottom strip gives the 90-day target

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Launching to everyone at once. A narrow first customer makes every other choice easier."}
```

chapters.title: CAGE distance
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **CAGE framework** measures how far a foreign market is from home in four ways: Cultural, Administrative, Geographic and Economic distance.

### Use it when

When a market entry case involves another country, to judge how hard the move will be.

### The parts

1. **Cultural:** Language, religion, tastes and habits. e.g. a beef-free menu that works in India may need changing abroad, and the reverse.
2. **Administrative:** Laws, trade rules, taxes, political ties. e.g. shared trade agreements make entry easier, hence lower distance.
3. **Geographic:** Physical distance, time zones, climate, transport. This matters most for heavy, fresh or fragile goods.
4. **Economic:** Gap in incomes, costs and infrastructure. e.g. a premium product priced for Europe may not fit a low-income market.
5. **Score and compare:** Rate each market low, medium or high on each distance. Thus we can rank countries, not just describe them.

### The framework

![CAGE distance: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f13_cage.png)

### On a slide

![CAGE distance: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s13_cage.png)

1. Title compares markets and picks one
2. Four equal columns, one per distance
3. Colour the distance that is the real hurdle
4. Bottom strip says how we handle it

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Looking only at market size. A big market can still be very far away."}
```

chapters.title: Mergers and acquisitions
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **M&A framework** decides whether buying another company makes sense by checking strategic fit, the price, the synergies and the risks of joining the two.

### Use it when

When a client wants to buy, merge with or invest in another company.

### The parts

1. **Why buy:** The goal: growth, new market, new product, capability or cost savings. e.g. a large FMCG firm buying a D2C brand to reach online buyers.
2. **Target's standalone value:** What the business is worth on its own, based on its profit and growth. This sets the base price.
3. **Synergies:** Extra value from combining: shared costs, cross-selling, buying power. e.g. selling the D2C brand through the buyer's 10 lakh stores.
4. **Price and returns:** Will the price paid leave room for a return after synergies? If we pay away all the synergies, the deal creates no value.
5. **Risks and integration:** Culture clash, staff leaving, hidden debt. Hence the plan for the first 100 days matters as much as the price.

### The framework

![Mergers and acquisitions: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f14_mergers.png)

### On a slide

![Mergers and acquisitions: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s14_mergers.png)

1. Title gives the walk-away price and why
2. Value build-up as bars, left to right
3. Colour the walk-away price only
4. So-what gives the headroom and the key risk

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Counting revenue synergies as certain. Cost synergies are far more reliable, so lean on them."}
```

chapters.title: Porter's five forces
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Porter's five forces** explains how profitable an industry can be by looking at five pressures: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power.

### Use it when

When the case asks if an industry is attractive, why margins are low, or whether to enter.

### The parts

1. **Rivalry among existing firms:** Many similar rivals fighting on price keep margins low. e.g. Indian airlines often compete hard on fares.
2. **Threat of new entrants:** Low barriers let new firms in. e.g. opening a cloud kitchen needs little money, hence new rivals appear constantly.
3. **Threat of substitutes:** Other ways to meet the same need. e.g. video calls are a substitute for business travel.
4. **Buyer power:** Strong buyers push prices down. e.g. large retail chains can squeeze small food brands for discounts and shelf fees.
5. **Supplier power:** Strong suppliers push costs up. e.g. a few makers of aircraft engines can set their prices.

### The framework

![Porter's five forces: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f15_five-forces.png)

### On a slide

![Porter's five forces: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s15_five-forces.png)

1. Title names the force that matters
2. Classic cross layout with equal box sizes
3. One force in coral, rated high
4. So-what turns the force into a move

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Rating all five forces as \"medium\". The point is to find the one or two forces that drive profit."}
```

chapters.title: 3Cs: company, customers, competitors
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **3Cs** look at a situation from three angles: the Company (what we are good at), the Customers (what they need) and the Competitors (what they offer).

### Use it when

For quick strategy questions, especially new products, positioning and "why are we losing share?" cases.

### The parts

1. **Customers:** Who they are, what they need, how they buy and what they value most. e.g. office workers buying lunch care most about speed.
2. **Company:** Our strengths, weaknesses, costs and assets. e.g. a chain with 200 outlets near offices has location as a strength.
3. **Competitors:** Who else serves the need, how well, and at what price. e.g. delivery apps meet the need for speed without a store.
4. **Find the overlap:** The winning space is what customers want, we do well and rivals do poorly. Thus the 3Cs point to a clear position.

### The framework

![3Cs: company, customers, competitors: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f16_three-cs.png)

### On a slide

![3Cs: company, customers, competitors: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s16_three-cs.png)

1. Title links need, strength and gap
2. Three circles, equal size, a clear overlap
3. Colour only the overlap we will own
4. So-what gives the promise and the proof

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Describing each C on its own. The value is in the overlap and the gap."}
```

chapters.title: SWOT
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**SWOT** lists a company's internal Strengths and Weaknesses, and the external Opportunities and Threats around it.

### Use it when

As a quick summary at the start or end of a strategy case. It works best when each point leads to an action.

### The parts

1. **Strengths:** Internal things we do well. e.g. a trusted brand and a wide distribution network.
2. **Weaknesses:** Internal things holding us back. e.g. an old product range or high cost per unit.
3. **Opportunities:** External trends we can use. e.g. rising demand for healthy snacks in cities.
4. **Threats:** External trends that can hurt us. e.g. a new low-price rival or a tax change.
5. **Make it TOWS:** Match the boxes: use strengths to grab opportunities, fix weaknesses that threats will expose. Thus a list becomes a plan.

### The framework

![SWOT: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f17_swot.png)

### On a slide

![SWOT: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s17_swot.png)

1. Title is the action, not "SWOT analysis"
2. Four boxes, three short points each at most
3. Colour the two boxes that pair into the action
4. So-what pairs two boxes into a plan

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "A SWOT with ten points per box and no conclusion. Three sharp points per box, then the so what."}
```

chapters.title: PESTEL
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**PESTEL** scans the big outside forces on a business: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal.

### Use it when

When a case involves a new country, a long time horizon, or a big change in the world around the industry.

### The parts

1. **Political:** Government stability, policy, subsidies. e.g. production-linked incentives that favour local electronics making.
2. **Economic:** Growth, inflation, interest rates, currency. e.g. higher interest rates slow car loans, hence car sales.
3. **Social:** Demographics, habits, values. e.g. more working women raises demand for ready-to-cook food.
4. **Technological:** New tools and platforms. e.g. UPI made small digital payments normal almost overnight.
5. **Environmental:** Climate, resources, sustainability rules. e.g. plastic bans changing packaging choices.
6. **Legal:** Laws on labour, data, safety and competition. e.g. data protection rules for apps.

### The framework

![PESTEL: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f18_pestel.png)

### On a slide

![PESTEL: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s18_pestel.png)

1. Title says which forces matter, not all six
2. Six equal columns with an impact rating
3. Colour the high-impact forces only
4. Bottom strip gives the action

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Filling all six letters with generic facts. Only forces that change the answer belong on the slide."}
```

chapters.title: BCG growth-share matrix
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **BCG matrix** places each business or product of a company on two scales, market growth and market share, to decide where to invest and where to pull back.

### Use it when

When a company has several products or units and must decide where to put its money.

### The parts

1. **Stars:** High share in a fast-growing market. They need investment to keep up, but are future cash cows.
2. **Cash cows:** High share in a slow market. They earn steady cash with little spend, hence they fund the rest.
3. **Question marks:** Low share in a fast market. Invest to grow them, or drop them; waiting is the worst option.
4. **Dogs:** Low share in a slow market. Usually sell, shrink or close. e.g. an old product line that ties up factory space.
5. **Balance the portfolio:** Use cash from cows to grow the best question marks into stars. Thus the company stays healthy over time.

### The framework

![BCG growth-share matrix: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f19_bcg.png)

### On a slide

![BCG growth-share matrix: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s19_bcg.png)

1. Title is the money move
2. 2x2 with plain axis labels; name the products inside each box
3. Colour the unit we invest in
4. So-what names the source of cash and the exits

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Using it for a single product company. The matrix only helps when there is a portfolio to balance."}
```

chapters.title: Competitive response
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **competitive response framework** decides how to react when a rival moves, such as a price cut or a new entrant, by first understanding the move and then choosing to ignore, match, differentiate or attack.

### Use it when

When the case starts with "a competitor has just...".

### The parts

1. **Understand the move:** What exactly changed, why the rival did it and can they keep it up? e.g. a start-up burning investor cash on 50% discounts may stop in six months.
2. **Measure the damage:** Which of our customers and products are at risk, and how much revenue? Often only one segment really moves.
3. **Ignore:** If the loss is small or the move will fade, do nothing. This saves margin.
4. **Match or defend:** Copy the move only where customers would leave. e.g. match price on the two items people compare, not on everything.
5. **Differentiate or attack:** Compete on what the rival cannot copy, such as service or range. Thus we avoid a price war we cannot win.

### The framework

![Competitive response: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f20_competitive-response.png)

### On a slide

![Competitive response: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s20_competitive-response.png)

1. Title gives the response and the real risk
2. Steps as one row, options at the end
3. Colour the response we pick
4. Bottom strip compares the cost of options

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Matching every move by reflex. Price wars hurt the strongest player least, and that may not be us."}
```

chapters.title: Blue Ocean (ERRC grid)
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**Blue Ocean strategy** looks for an uncontested market space; the **ERRC grid** gets there by deciding what to Eliminate, Reduce, Raise and Create compared with the industry.

### Use it when

When an industry is crowded and everyone competes on the same things, or when the case asks for a new business idea.

### The parts

1. **Eliminate:** Things the industry takes for granted that customers do not value. e.g. a budget hotel removing the restaurant and lobby.
2. **Reduce:** Things to offer below the industry standard. e.g. smaller rooms.
3. **Raise:** Things to offer well above the standard. e.g. a better bed and faster Wi-Fi.
4. **Create:** Things the industry has never offered. e.g. booking and check-in fully on the phone.
5. **Value curve:** Plot our offer against rivals on each factor. A different shape means a different market, hence less direct rivalry.

### The framework

![Blue Ocean (ERRC grid): the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f21_blue-ocean.png)

### On a slide

![Blue Ocean (ERRC grid): slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s21_blue-ocean.png)

1. Title gives the new offer and its economics
2. Four boxes, two or three words each
3. Colour the Create box, the new idea
4. So-what gives cost and customer proof

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Only adding features (raise and create). The cost advantage comes from eliminate and reduce."}
```

chapters.title: STP: segment, target, position
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

**STP** means we split the market into groups with similar needs (Segmentation), choose which groups to serve (Targeting), and decide how we want them to see us (Positioning).

### Use it when

When a case asks who to sell to, how to reposition a brand, or why a product is not selling.

### The parts

1. **Segmentation:** Split buyers by needs, behaviour, age, income or place. e.g. car buyers split into first-time buyers, families and enthusiasts.
2. **Targeting:** Pick the segments that are big, growing, reachable and where we can win. e.g. first-time buyers in tier-2 cities.
3. **Positioning:** One clear idea we want to own in their mind. e.g. "the safest car in its price band".
4. **Positioning map:** Plot brands on the two factors buyers care about most. The empty space on the map shows where to position.

### The framework

![STP: segment, target, position: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f22_stp.png)

### On a slide

![STP: segment, target, position: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s22_stp.png)

1. Title names segment and position together
2. Three steps across, each one box
3. Colour the target choice
4. Bottom strip gives the proof

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Targeting everyone. A position that tries to appeal to all segments says nothing to any of them."}
```

chapters.title: Marketing mix: 4Ps
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **4Ps** are the four decisions every product needs: Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

### Use it when

When the case asks how to launch, fix or grow a product, once we know who the target customer is.

### The parts

1. **Product:** What we sell: features, quality, design, pack sizes. e.g. shampoo in ₹2 sachets so rural buyers can try it.
2. **Price:** What we charge and how: list price, discounts, payment terms. This must fit the target customer's budget and the value they see.
3. **Place:** Where the customer can buy it: stores, online, distributors. e.g. a snack brand needs kirana shops, not just supermarkets, to reach small towns.
4. **Promotion:** How customers hear about it: ads, influencers, sampling, offers. e.g. free samples at a cricket match for a new energy drink.
5. **Check the fit:** All four must tell the same story. Thus a premium product does not sit in a discount bin.

### The framework

![Marketing mix: 4Ps: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f23_four-ps.png)

### On a slide

![Marketing mix: 4Ps: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s23_four-ps.png)

1. Title says which P is broken
2. Four equal columns, a verdict under each
3. Colour the P that needs fixing
4. Bottom strip gives the first action

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Treating the Ps one by one. The answer is usually one broken P, or two that contradict each other."}
```

chapters.title: Services mix: 7Ps
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **7Ps** extend the 4Ps for services by adding People, Process and Physical evidence, because a service is made and used at the same time.

### Use it when

For cases on restaurants, hotels, banks, hospitals, airlines, education and any business where the customer meets staff.

### The parts

1. **The first four:** Product, Price, Place and Promotion work as in the 4Ps.
2. **People:** Staff who deliver the service, and how they are hired and trained. e.g. a hotel's front desk shapes the whole stay.
3. **Process:** The steps the customer goes through, and how smooth they are. e.g. a hospital's waiting time from arrival to doctor.
4. **Physical evidence:** What the customer can see and touch that proves quality: the space, uniforms, the app. e.g. a clean, bright clinic signals good care.
5. **Find the weak link:** One bad step spoils the experience. Hence we map the customer's path and fix the worst moment first.

### The framework

![Services mix: 7Ps: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f24_seven-ps.png)

### On a slide

![Services mix: 7Ps: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s24_seven-ps.png)

1. Title names the weak P and its number
2. Seven around one centre, equal sizes
3. Colour the weak P only
4. So-what gives the fix and what to delay

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Forgetting that the customer sees the whole service. A great product with a slow process still feels bad."}
```

chapters.title: Customer funnel (AARRR)
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **customer funnel** tracks how many people move through each stage from first hearing about us to paying again; the AARRR version names the stages Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral and Revenue.

### Use it when

When the case is about an app, website or brand that gets attention but not sales, or sales but no repeat.

### The parts

1. **Acquisition:** People who find us: visits, downloads, store footfall. e.g. 1 lakh app downloads in a month.
2. **Activation:** People who have a good first experience. e.g. users who place a first order.
3. **Retention:** People who come back. e.g. users who order again within 30 days.
4. **Referral:** People who bring others. e.g. users who share an invite code.
5. **Revenue:** People who pay, and how much. Thus we see where money is made.
6. **Find the leak:** Compare conversion at each step with benchmarks; the biggest drop is the problem. Hence more ads cannot fix a leak further down.

### The framework

![Customer funnel (AARRR): the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f25_funnel.png)

### On a slide

![Customer funnel (AARRR): slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s25_funnel.png)

1. Title gives the leak and the order of action
2. Funnel bars shrink to scale, one number each
3. Colour the leaking stage
4. So-what gives the benchmark and the value

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Measuring only the top of the funnel. Downloads look good on a slide but pay nothing."}
```

chapters.title: Value chain
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **value chain** lists every activity a company performs to create and deliver its product, so we can see where it adds value and where it spends most.

### Use it when

When the case asks where a company's advantage comes from, where costs sit, or what to outsource.

### The parts

1. **Inbound logistics:** Receiving and storing inputs. e.g. a dairy collecting milk from villages every morning.
2. **Operations:** Turning inputs into the product. e.g. pasteurising and packing the milk.
3. **Outbound logistics:** Getting the product to buyers. e.g. cold trucks to shops before 6 am.
4. **Marketing and sales:** Making people want it and buy it. e.g. brand ads and retailer schemes.
5. **Service:** Support after the sale. e.g. replacing spoiled packs quickly.
6. **Support activities:** HR, technology, buying and management that help every step. Thus advantage can hide in support too, such as a better procurement team.

### The framework

![Value chain: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f26_value-chain.png)

### On a slide

![Value chain: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s26_value-chain.png)

1. Title names the step that creates the edge
2. Five arrows in a row, support band below
3. Colour the step that wins
4. Bottom strip says where to invest and what to outsource

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Listing activities without judging them. Mark each step as an advantage, at par, or a weakness."}
```

chapters.title: McKinsey 7S
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **7S model** checks whether seven parts of an organisation fit together: Strategy, Structure, Systems, Shared values, Style, Staff and Skills.

### Use it when

When the case is about a merger, a new strategy that is not working, or a big change inside a company.

### The parts

1. **Hard S: Strategy, Structure, Systems:** The plan, the org chart and the processes. These are easy to change on paper.
2. **Soft S: Style, Staff, Skills:** How leaders behave, who works there and what they can do. e.g. a digital plan fails if staff lack digital skills.
3. **Shared values:** The core beliefs at the centre that hold the rest together. e.g. a family firm's value of caution may clash with a fast-growth strategy.
4. **Find the misfit:** Look for the S that does not match the others. Hence we fix the cause of the problem, not the symptom.

### The framework

![McKinsey 7S: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f27_seven-s.png)

### On a slide

![McKinsey 7S: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s27_seven-s.png)

1. Title names the S that does not fit
2. Six around the centre, equal spacing
3. Colour the misfit only
4. So-what gives the fix and the time

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Describing all seven Ss. The insight is the one that does not fit."}
```

chapters.title: Business Model Canvas
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **Business Model Canvas** describes how a business works on one page, in nine blocks: customers, value, channels, relationships, revenue, resources, activities, partners and costs.

### Use it when

When the case asks us to explain, design or change a business model, often for start-ups.

### The parts

1. **Customer side:** Customer segments, value proposition, channels and relationships: who we serve, what we promise, how we reach and keep them.
2. **Money in:** Revenue streams: how and when customers pay. e.g. a gym earns from monthly plans and from personal training.
3. **Engine side:** Key resources, key activities and key partners: what we need, do and borrow to deliver. e.g. a cloud kitchen's partners are the delivery apps.
4. **Money out:** Cost structure: the biggest costs of running the model. e.g. commissions to delivery apps can be 20 to 30% of an order.
5. **Test the links:** Each block should support the others. Thus a weak block, like a channel that eats the margin, is easy to spot.

### The framework

![Business Model Canvas: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f28_business-model-canvas.png)

### On a slide

![Business Model Canvas: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s28_business-model-canvas.png)

1. Title names the block that breaks the model
2. Nine blocks in the standard layout, short words only
3. Colour the weak block
4. Bottom strip gives the fix with a target

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Filling the canvas like a form. Use it to find the one block that holds the business back."}
```

chapters.title: Make or buy (outsourcing)
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **make or buy framework** decides whether to do an activity in-house or pay someone else, by comparing cost, quality, control and how core the activity is.

### Use it when

When a case asks whether to outsource, build a factory, or bring something back in-house.

### The parts

1. **Is it core:** If the activity is what makes us different, keep it. e.g. a coffee chain keeps its bean blend recipe; it can outsource cleaning.
2. **Cost:** Compare full in-house cost (including space, people and management time) with the supplier's price. e.g. a supplier with scale may be 20% cheaper.
3. **Quality and control:** Can a supplier meet our standard reliably? This matters most for things customers notice.
4. **Risk and flexibility:** Outsourcing makes costs flexible but adds dependency. Hence we check supplier strength and switching cost.

### The framework

![Make or buy (outsourcing): the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f29_make-or-buy.png)

### On a slide

![Make or buy (outsourcing): slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s29_make-or-buy.png)

1. Title gives the decision and both reasons
2. 2x2 with plain axis labels and short box names
3. Colour the box the activity falls in
4. So-what gives the saving and the risk control

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Comparing the supplier's price with only our direct cost. Hidden overheads make in-house look cheaper than it is."}
```

chapters.title: Operations and bottlenecks
chapters.markdown:
### In one line

The **operations framework** maps the steps a product or customer goes through, measures how much each step can handle, and finds the **bottleneck**: the slowest step, which limits the whole process.

### Use it when

When the case is about long waits, low output, delays, or a factory, kitchen, hospital or warehouse that cannot keep up.

### The parts

1. **Map the process:** Write each step in order. e.g. a restaurant: order, cook, plate, serve, bill.
2. **Measure capacity:** How many units each step can handle per hour. e.g. the kitchen cooks 60 meals an hour, but billing handles only 40.
3. **Find the bottleneck:** The step with the lowest capacity sets the pace for everything. Hence speeding up any other step changes nothing.
4. **Fix it:** Add capacity, cut time per unit, or move work away from it. e.g. pay at the table by QR code.
5. **Check the next one:** Once fixed, the bottleneck moves to the next slowest step. Thus improvement is a loop, not a one-off.

### The framework

![Operations and bottlenecks: the framework](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/f30_operations.png)

### On a slide

![Operations and bottlenecks: slide storyboard](content/prep/files/case-toolkit/s30_operations.png)

1. Title names the bottleneck and the fix
2. One bar per step, same scale, labelled directly
3. Colour the shortest bar only
4. So-what says what limits us next

```msv-block
{"type": "callout", "heading": "Watch out", "icon": "fa-triangle-exclamation", "text": "Speeding up the step that looks busiest instead of the one with the lowest capacity."}
```

chapters.title: Words to know
chapters.markdown:
Terms used across the guide, each with a plain meaning and an example.

| Term | What it means | e.g. |
|---|---|---|
| **Action title** | A slide title written as a full sentence that states the answer. | "Logistics cost explains the margin gap" instead of "Cost analysis". |
| **Hypothesis** | Our best early guess at the answer, stated so data can prove it wrong. | "Profit fell because fuel cost rose." |
| **MECE** | Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive: no overlaps, nothing missing. | Splitting profit into revenue and cost. |
| **So what** | The meaning of a fact for the decision. | "Repeat rate is 20%" → so we fix retention before ads. |
| **White space** | The empty area of a slide that frames the content. | A 5% margin on every side. |
| **Contribution** | Price minus variable cost; what each unit adds towards fixed cost and profit. | ₹150 coffee − ₹50 inputs = ₹100. |
| **Benchmark** | A comparison point, such as a rival or last year. | Our delivery cost 12% vs rival 7%. |
| **Synergy** | Extra value from combining two businesses. | Selling the bought brand through our stores. |
| **Churn** | The share of customers who stop buying in a period. | 5% of subscribers cancel each month. |
| **Segment** | A group of buyers with similar needs. | First-time car buyers. |
